passage:
The doctrine of informed consent, as it has evolved in Anglo-American medical law, rests on a deceptively simple premise: a patient cannot meaningfully authorize a medical procedure without first receiving adequate disclosure of its risks, benefits, and alternatives. Courts in the twentieth century elaborated this premise into a demanding standard, holding that physicians bear an affirmative duty to disclose whatever a reasonable patient would consider material to the treatment decision. The landmark Canterbury v. Spence ruling articulated this patient-centered standard, explicitly rejecting the older professional-custom standard under which adequacy of disclosure was measured by what a reasonable physician would typically reveal.

The shift matters because the two standards produce different outcomes in contested cases. Under the professional-custom standard, physicians could effectively define the scope of disclosure for their own profession—a self-referential arrangement critics found paternalistic. The patient-centered standard transfers evaluative authority to a hypothetical lay patient, forcing courts to ask what information a nonexpert would regard as significant. This reorientation has had substantial practical consequences: physicians who omit statistical risk data, fail to mention less invasive alternatives, or neglect to discuss experimental options may now face liability even if colleagues in their specialty routinely do the same. Informed consent, on this account, is as much a doctrine of patients' epistemic rights as it is a doctrine of tort liability.
comparativeBPassage:
A widespread assumption in bioethics holds that informed consent is the cornerstone of respect for patient autonomy. While that aspiration is admirable, the legal doctrine that carries its name has been progressively hollowed out in practice. Empirical studies consistently show that most patients cannot recall the substantive content of consent forms they signed minutes earlier, and that signature rates remain near universal regardless of the complexity of the disclosed risks. If the purpose of informed consent is to produce genuinely autonomous decision-making, the current procedural apparatus—lengthy forms, rushed disclosures, checkboxes—fails on its own terms.

The root difficulty is that legal informed consent conflates two distinct functions: the authorization function (securing valid legal permission for a procedure) and the deliberative function (enabling thoughtful patient decision-making). Courts, preoccupied with liability allocation, have optimized almost exclusively for the authorization function. The result is a doctrine that generates paper trails rather than understanding. Some bioethicists have proposed replacing or supplementing standard disclosure with interactive dialogue models—structured conversations in which clinicians assess and respond to the individual patient's actual level of comprehension. Such models are costly and difficult to implement at scale, but they at least address the deliberative function that the legal doctrine has abandoned. Until consent procedures are redesigned around the patient's cognitive experience rather than the physician's legal exposure, informed consent will remain a procedural formality rather than a genuine exercise of autonomy.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following questions is most central to both passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: What procedural reforms would make consent forms easier for patients to understand?

choices.label: B
choices.text: How adequately does current informed-consent doctrine serve the interests of patients?

choices.label: C
choices.text: In what circumstances can a physician be held liable for failure to disclose risks?

choices.label: D
choices.text: What is the historical origin of the patient-centered disclosure standard?

choices.label: E
choices.text: How do courts determine what information a reasonable patient would consider material?

explanations.correct: Passage A traces the evolution of informed-consent doctrine as a vehicle for protecting patient interests; passage B argues that the doctrine fails patients in practice. Both passages are organized around evaluating how well the doctrine actually serves patients.
explanations.A: Only passage B raises procedural reforms; passage A does not address them.
explanations.B: Correct. Both passages assess the doctrine from the patient's perspective—A approvingly, B critically.
explanations.C: Liability conditions are discussed in passage A but are not the central concern of passage B.
explanations.D: Historical origin is mentioned only in passage A as background, not as the central question of either passage.
explanations.E: The reasonable-patient standard is a detail in passage A, not a question either passage treats as primary.

questions.questionStem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to disagree over which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: whether the professional-custom standard gave physicians too much control over disclosure decisions

choices.label: B
choices.text: whether the patient-centered standard represents a meaningful improvement over its predecessor

choices.label: C
choices.text: whether patients have any legitimate interest in receiving information about treatment alternatives

choices.label: D
choices.text: whether courts have played a role in shaping informed-consent doctrine

choices.label: E
choices.text: whether informed consent is related to the concept of patient autonomy

explanations.correct: Passage A presents the patient-centered standard as a genuine advance—transferring authority to the lay patient and expanding liability where disclosure is inadequate. Passage B argues that even under the evolved doctrine, the practice produces paperwork rather than understanding, implying the improvement is largely illusory in real-world effect.
explanations.A: Passage A criticizes the professional-custom standard as paternalistic, and passage B does not defend it; neither author endorses it.
explanations.B: Correct. Passage A is broadly approving of the evolved standard; passage B argues it has been hollowed out in practice.
explanations.C: Both passages assume patients have a legitimate interest in information; they differ on whether current doctrine delivers it.
explanations.D: Both passages acknowledge courts' role; there is no disagreement here.
explanations.E: Both passages link informed consent to autonomy; this is shared ground.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following is mentioned in passage B but not in passage A?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the distinction between a patient-centered and a professional-custom disclosure standard

choices.label: B
choices.text: the role of courts in defining the scope of physician liability

choices.label: C
choices.text: empirical data showing that patients forget consent-form content shortly after signing

choices.label: D
choices.text: the principle that patients possess a right to information about treatment alternatives

choices.label: E
choices.text: the Canterbury v. Spence ruling as a turning point in disclosure law

explanations.correct: Passage B explicitly cites empirical studies showing patients cannot recall disclosed risks shortly after signing. Passage A makes no reference to empirical research on patient recall.
explanations.A: The distinction between the two standards is the organizing theme of passage A's second paragraph.
explanations.B: Courts' role in shaping liability is discussed in passage A as well as passage B.
explanations.C: Correct. Only passage B introduces empirical recall data.
explanations.D: Passage A states that informed consent encompasses patients' epistemic rights, including information about alternatives.
explanations.E: Canterbury v. Spence appears only in passage A.

questions.questionStem: It can be inferred from passage B that the author would most likely regard interactive dialogue models of consent as

choices.label: A
choices.text: a fully satisfactory replacement for current consent procedures in all clinical settings

choices.label: B
choices.text: an impractical proposal that should be abandoned in favor of improved written forms

choices.label: C
choices.text: a promising but logistically difficult approach that addresses the gap current doctrine ignores

choices.label: D
choices.text: an unnecessary measure given that patients already understand the risks disclosed to them

choices.label: E
choices.text: a model whose benefits are limited to patients with prior medical knowledge

explanations.correct: Passage B says interactive dialogue models are 'costly and difficult to implement at scale' (limiting their practicality) but that 'they at least address the deliberative function that the legal doctrine has abandoned'—a guarded endorsement consistent with answer C.
explanations.A: The passage qualifies its endorsement with 'costly and difficult to implement at scale,' ruling out a fully satisfactory characterization.
explanations.B: The author does not recommend abandoning the idea; the passage calls it a genuine address to the deliberative function.
explanations.C: Correct. 'Costly and difficult' captures the logistical concern; 'at least address the deliberative function' captures the promise.
explanations.D: The passage explicitly states patients cannot recall disclosed risks, contradicting this choice.
explanations.E: The passage mentions individual patient comprehension generally, without restricting benefits to medically knowledgeable patients.

questions.questionStem: In passage A, the reference to Canterbury v. Spence primarily serves to

choices.label: A
choices.text: introduce a legal case whose outcome passage A will ultimately criticize

choices.label: B
choices.text: illustrate that the patient-centered standard displaced a standard the author regards as paternalistic

choices.label: C
choices.text: provide an example of a case in which a physician was found liable for inadequate disclosure

choices.label: D
choices.text: suggest that most courts have refused to adopt the patient-centered standard

choices.label: E
choices.text: demonstrate that informed consent originated as a doctrine of tort liability rather than autonomy

explanations.correct: The Canterbury v. Spence reference is used to anchor the claim that courts shifted from a professional-custom standard (later characterized as paternalistic) to the patient-centered standard. Its function is to concretize the doctrinal shift passage A endorses.
explanations.A: Passage A does not criticize Canterbury; it presents the case approvingly as a landmark.
explanations.B: Correct. The case illustrates the rejection of the older, physician-controlled standard that passage A calls paternalistic.
explanations.C: The passage does not detail the specific facts or liability outcome of Canterbury; it characterizes the standard the case articulated.
explanations.D: The passage suggests the opposite—that the patient-centered standard is now the law—not that courts have refused it.
explanations.E: Passage A's final sentence positions informed consent as a doctrine of epistemic rights, not merely liability.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the two passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Passage A describes a legal doctrine and its historical evolution; passage B argues that a practical failure in that doctrine's implementation undermines its stated purpose.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Passage A proposes a reform to an existing legal standard; passage B supplies empirical evidence that the reform has succeeded.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Passage A presents one side of a legal dispute; passage B presents the opposing party's arguments in the same dispute.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Passage A defends a philosophical concept; passage B rejects that concept and proposes an entirely different framework.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Passage A identifies a problem with informed-consent doctrine; passage B offers a historical account of how that problem arose.

explanations.correct: Passage A traces the doctrinal evolution from the professional-custom to the patient-centered standard approvingly; passage B accepts the doctrine as established but argues that its real-world implementation—paper forms, rushed disclosures—undermines the autonomy it is supposed to protect.
explanations.A: Correct. 'Describes and its evolution' fits A; 'practical failure undermines stated purpose' fits B.
explanations.B: Passage A does not propose a reform—it describes one that already occurred. Passage B does not argue the reform succeeded; it argues the opposite.
explanations.C: The passages are not accounts of opposing parties in a single legal dispute.
explanations.D: Passage B does not reject the concept of patient autonomy; it argues current doctrine fails to realize it. Nor does it propose an entirely different framework—it suggests supplementing existing procedures.
explanations.E: The identification of a problem is passage B's role, not A's; A is largely descriptive and approving.

questions.questionStem: The author of passage B would be most likely to make which one of the following criticisms of the claim, made in passage A, that the patient-centered standard meaningfully protects patients' epistemic rights?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The patient-centered standard is unconstitutional because it imposes obligations on physicians that exceed the bounds of tort law.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The patient-centered standard actually makes disclosure decisions more paternalistic than the professional-custom standard it replaced.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Optimizing disclosure for legal authorization rather than genuine comprehension means the standard protects rights only on paper.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The standard is applied inconsistently across jurisdictions, so its protective effect is geographically limited.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The hypothetical reasonable patient is an inappropriate standard because most patients have no medical training.

explanations.correct: Passage B's central criticism is that the legal doctrine has been optimized for the authorization function—generating paper trails and legal permission—at the expense of the deliberative function that would produce genuine comprehension. This directly challenges passage A's claim that the standard protects epistemic rights.
explanations.A: Passage B makes no constitutional argument; its critique is practical and philosophical, not legal-authority based.
explanations.B: Passage B does not argue the patient-centered standard is more paternalistic than its predecessor; it argues the standard is procedurally empty regardless of which party it nominally centers.
explanations.C: Correct. Passage B explicitly contrasts the authorization function (legal permission) with the deliberative function (real understanding), arguing courts have neglected the latter.
explanations.D: Jurisdictional inconsistency is not mentioned in passage B; this is an outside-scope trap.
explanations.E: Passage B's criticism is about the gap between legal procedure and cognitive reality, not about the reasonableness of the hypothetical-patient standard per se.
